author: D.M. Martins Research
title: Many retail investors probably follow the old advice (suppor
text:
Many retail investors probably follow the old advice (supported by the likes of Warren Buffett ) and allocate most, if not all, of their equity investments into an inexpensive fund that tracks the performance of the S&P 500 ( SPY ).
I believe using such an approach to growing one's portfolio over time is a smart one at face value. Consider that buying the S&P 500 allows for diversification into hundreds of names that nearly eliminates unsystematic risk . It also saves investors hundreds of hours' worth of research needed to make an informed decision on what stocks to buy, which could be otherwise spent in a more productive way (like working a second job, volunteering or taking a nap).
But there's much more to the story. If you subscribe to the idea above and own shares of an S&P 500 index fund, the bad news is that you may be holding on to an unbalanced stock portfolio.

Image credit 
How is this possible? Let me introduce you to the graph below. It represents the sector allocation of the S&P 500 over time, since 1990.

Source: Bespoke 
There are a couple of things that might have caught your attention immediately. First, a large proportion of the index, 51% to be exact, is currently made up of stocks in only three key sectors: technology (20%), financials (16%) and healthcare (15%). Second, tech stocks have appreciated relatively more rapidly over the past 30 years, and now account for about one-fifth of the index from only 6% in 1990. Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Facebook ( FB ) alone are worth more than 10% of the S&P 500.
